subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 14 periods = 700 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 11h 40min

periods.activity_title: Before the Curtain Rises: Music, Tradition and Expectation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.169): identify stringed instruments by first letter, pair work
Reflect and Respond (p.169): share instrument of choice and reason, open discussion
Reflect and Respond (p.169): discuss generational differences in music preference

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick paired exchange on stringed instruments — students identify examples by first letter, drawing on what they already know. Establish the shared vocabulary of classical and modern music before the play begins.

Whole-class discussion: would students choose a classical instrument or a modern one, and why? Elicit personal reasons and emotional stakes, building the frame of individual choice versus family expectation.

Guide a focused exchange on whether children and elders in students' own families share musical tastes. Draw out reasons — tradition, generation, exposure — so the class enters the play primed for Shruti's dilemma.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening discussion grounds students in the tradition-versus-modernity tension that drives the entire play. Students often make the generational gap abstract; press them for a specific family example to make it concrete before the text is read. No prior knowledge of the play is assumed or needed here.
materials: Textbook pp.169–193 (Twin Melodies, for reference to instrument names)

periods.activity_title: Act I Read Aloud: Fusion, Fear and the Newspaper Review

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.170): complete figurative-phrase paragraph, discuss literal vs figurative meaning

time_bands.activity: Assign parts — Shruti, Iqbal, Avinash, Peter, and a narrator for stage directions — and read Act I aloud (pp.169–175), observing asides and parenthetical delivery cues. Pause briefly after the newspaper-review moment to let the tonal shift register.

Work in pairs on the figurative-phrase paragraph from Reflect and Respond (p.170): students fill the blanks with phrases from the box, then discuss with the teacher whether each phrase carries a literal or figurative meaning. Whole-class debrief names which phrases echo the play's own emotional register.

periods.teacher_notes: The aside marked for Shruti in Act I is pivotal — ensure the student reading her part delivers it in a lowered, confiding voice, distinct from the ensemble cheer around her. The figurative-phrase task works best when students first attempt the blanks cold and then revise after the discussion, rather than consulting the play text immediately.

periods.activity_title: Act I Close Reading: Setting, Characters and Dialogue

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.174): complete Act I table — setting, instruments, speaker-dialogue-reason
Reflect and Respond (p.174): predict whether Shruti will gather courage, give a reason
Reflect and Respond (p.174): predict Shruti's father's likely reaction and reason

time_bands.activity: Students individually complete the Act I comprehension table (p.174): setting details, each child's instrument, and the three-column speaker–words–reason analysis. Teacher circulates and checks entries before moving to whole-class verification.

Pairs discuss whether Shruti will find the courage to speak to her father, drawing only on what Act I reveals about her character and her father's reputation. Students share one-sentence reasons; teacher notes the range of predictions on the board.

Open the question of what Shruti's father's reaction might be and why. Students infer from Shruti's own fear — 'I just don't know how to tell him in the right way' — to build a profile of Nabin before Act II is read.

periods.teacher_notes: The three-column dialogue table in the comprehension exercise requires students to distinguish between what a speaker says and why — a distinction that also underpins the Critical Reflection questions later. Students frequently fill the 'reason' column with plot summary rather than character motivation; redirect toward the character's internal state. Predictions about the father should stay grounded in textual evidence from Act I, not general assumptions.

periods.activity_title: Act II Read Aloud: The Dinner Table Confrontation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.178): complete Act II summary using words from the box

time_bands.activity: Assign roles — Shruti, Nabin, Leela, narrator — and read Act II aloud (pp.175–178), observing stage directions including Shruti's untouched dosa and Nabin's exit. The student reading Nabin should project firmness rather than anger; coach the delivery before the act begins.

Students complete the Act II summary cloze (p.178) individually, choosing from the word box; teacher leads whole-class verification. Conclude with a brief discussion of which words most precisely capture Nabin's manner — 'firm' versus 'surprised', 'disapproval' versus 'setback' — to sharpen the class's sense of his register.

periods.teacher_notes: Nabin's line about Shruti 'drowning her individual style in the hubbub of an orchestra' is the thematic crux of Act II and should be read slowly, with a pause before the class moves on. The cloze exercise distinguishes between plot words and character-register words; pressing students on why 'firm' fits better than 'surprised' builds the analytical vocabulary they will need for the Critical Reflection questions.

periods.activity_title: Between Acts: Predicting Reconciliation in Act III

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.178): predict whether Shruti's father will attend the rehearsal, with reason
Reflect and Respond (p.178): discuss whether Shruti and her parents will reach mutual understanding

time_bands.activity: Open with the prediction question: will Nabin attend the rehearsal? Students write a one-sentence answer with a reason drawn from Act II, then share in pairs. Teacher invites two or three pairs to present contrasting predictions, keeping the discussion text-bound.

Widen the discussion: do students think Shruti and her parents can reach genuine mutual understanding, or will the gap remain? Invite students to cite specific moments from Acts I and II — Shruti's promise to Leela, Nabin's mockery — as evidence for their positions.

Brief whole-class synthesis: teacher notes the class's predictions on the board and asks what would need to change — in Nabin, in Shruti, or in the situation — for reconciliation to happen. This frames Act III as a purposeful reading event.

periods.teacher_notes: Shruti's Act II promise — 'I will never hide again' — is the emotional hinge between Act II and Act III; encouraging students to notice it here sharpens the payoff when Nabin arrives unannounced at the rehearsal. Predictions should remain grounded in textual evidence rather than general optimism about family harmony.

periods.activity_title: Act III Read Aloud and True/False Comprehension Check

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.181–182): identify true statements about Act III events and Nabin's arc

time_bands.activity: Assign parts — Shruti, Nabin, Leela, Iqbal, Avinash, Peter, narrator — and read Act III aloud (pp.178–183), paying close attention to stage directions: Nabin tapping his feet, clapping furiously, and Leela's quiet aside about Nabin's own past. Deliver the aside at near-whisper.

Students individually assess the six true/false statements (p.181–182) about Act III events and Nabin's character arc. Teacher leads verification, pressing students to name the precise moment in Act III that confirms or contradicts each statement rather than relying on general impression.

periods.teacher_notes: Leela's revelation that Nabin himself defied his traditional vocalist family to take up the violin is the play's structural parallel and must not pass quickly; after the act is read, ask the class what this history explains about Nabin's earlier rigidity before moving to the true/false exercise. Students often mark the statement about Nabin 'following family tradition as a violinist' as true — probe why it is false, since violin was the break from tradition.

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection: Extract Analysis Across Both Key Moments

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.182–183): two extracts — close-reading sub-questions on dilemma, language and theme

homework.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.184): six extended-answer questions — title justification, character analysis, theme

time_bands.activity: Distribute the two extract passages from Critical Reflection (p.182–183) — Shruti's dilemma exchange with Iqbal, and Nabin's breakthrough admission. Students read silently and annotate any words or phrases that feel emotionally charged or thematically significant.

Work through Extract 1 sub-questions as a class: Shruti's state of mind, the meaning of 'the right way', the generational-gap dimension, and Iqbal's function as reassurance. Teacher models how to move from initial impression to a close reading of exact word choice.

Students work in pairs on Extract 2 sub-questions — Nabin's breakthrough, the double meaning of 'lost', the hug as dramatic gesture, inference about Shruti's future, and identifying the phrase 'each bay, its own wind'. Pairs share answers; teacher consolidates the analytical vocabulary before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrase 'each bay, its own wind' is the play's most compressed thematic statement; students should be asked to explain it in their own words before the unit closes, as it will anchor the title-justification question in the extended-answer homework. The Extract 2 question about the word 'duty' — which does not convey reconciliation — is a genuine evaluative move and should not be treated as a simple recall item.

periods.activity_title: Drama Language: Asides, Fillers, Music Vocabulary and Phrases

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.184): MCQ on function of 'aside' in drama
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.185): non-lexical fillers — function MCQ and emoticon-matching
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): match music-related words to meanings
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): write meanings of three phrases — 'drown your individual style', 'sense of musicality', 'go down the drain'

time_bands.activity: Read Shruti's aside aloud from p.184 and pose the MCQ on its function; students respond then discuss how the aside differs from a normal line — what it reveals about Shruti that ordinary dialogue cannot. Connect to Leela's Act III aside about Nabin's past.

Examine non-lexical fillers ('Ahem ahem', 'I…er…') from the play text: students answer the MCQ on their function, then match each emoticon to the correct filler from the box — whew, err, arrgh, hmmm, ahem-ahem. Debrief with a quick round where students supply the right filler for a scenario the teacher reads aloud.

Students individually match the seven music-related terms (rhythm, tempo, bass, baritone, cacophony, pitch, scale) to their definitions (p.186). Teacher verifies answers and invites students to find each word in the play or in everyday musical talk.

Students write the meanings of 'drown your individual style', 'sense of musicality', and 'go down the drain' in their own words, using context from the play and the sentences on p.186. Two or three students share; the class refines where needed.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate 'aside' with a soliloquy; the distinction — one is a brief private thought overheard by the audience, the other is an extended speech — is worth pinning down here before the writing task in a later unit requires students to include an aside of their own. The music-vocabulary matching task becomes richer if students are asked to locate each term in the play text rather than simply matching definitions in isolation.
materials: Textbook pp.184–186 (Vocabulary and Structures in Context, Twin Melodies)

periods.activity_title: Grammar in Context: Exclamatory to Declarative and Reported Speech

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.187): identify exclamatory sentences; convert to declarative using 'exclaimed'
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.187): convert six play dialogues to reported speech

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.188): report Asma–Deepa dialogue in indirect speech, complete four blanks

time_bands.activity: Pose the two exclamatory sentences from p.187 and elicit the sentence-type MCQ answer. Teacher models the conversion of one sentence — removing the interjection, dropping the exclamation mark, and inserting 'exclaimed with joy' — before students convert the second sentence independently.

Teacher works through the reported-speech conversion of dialogues 1–3 from p.187 on the board, highlighting tense shift and pronoun change at each step. Students complete dialogues 4–6 in writing; teacher circulates and addresses common errors — retained direct-speech pronouns, missed tense backshift.

Pairs swap their dialogues 4–6 for a quick peer check, focusing on whether the interjection has been removed and the reporting verb is appropriate. Teacher addresses any persistent error pattern with two corrected examples before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The use of 'exclaimed' and 'exclaimed with (feeling)' is specific to exclamatory-to-declarative conversion — students frequently default to 'said', which flattens the emotional register. The reported-speech sentences are all drawn from the play's own cast (Shruti, Leela, Avinash, Iqbal), so connecting each transformation back to the character's moment in the play keeps the grammar purposeful rather than mechanical.
materials: Textbook pp.187–188 (Vocabulary and Structures in Context, Twin Melodies)

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Musician: The Yazh and Its Heritage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.189): look at stringed instruments and decide which could be the yazh
Listen and Respond (p.189): listen to musician describing the yazh, verify instrument choice
Listen and Respond (p.189): listen again and complete notes with not more than three words per blank

time_bands.activity: Students look at the printed images of stringed instruments on p.189 and in pairs decide which could be the yazh, reasoning from visual shape and what they have learnt about ancient Indian instruments. Brief whole-class share — note the range of guesses before the audio is played.

Teacher reads the transcript (p.270) aloud in the role of the musician, at an unhurried pace. Students verify whether their instrument choice was correct, then discuss briefly what in the description confirmed or surprised them.

Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students complete the structured notes (p.189) — instrument type, ancient context, predecessor, design features (stem tip, resonator shape and material), and the four named variety types. Teacher verifies answers with the class, ensuring no blank exceeds three words.

periods.teacher_notes: The yazh connects to the play's broader theme of musical heritage: the instrument's journey from ancient Tamil music to near-obscurity mirrors the tension between preserving classical forms and allowing new ones. Students may be unfamiliar with the term 'resonator'; briefly glossing it as the body that amplifies sound before the second listening prevents a comprehension gap.
materials: Textbook pp.189 (Listen and Respond, Twin Melodies)

periods.activity_title: Voice in the Play: Stress, Intonation and Emotional Delivery

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.189–190): perform four play lines with indicated stress and intonation; discuss emotional impact

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the first line — 'I don't want papa to feel that I don't care about his opinions, because I do' — twice: once with stress on 'don't care' and once on 'because I do'. Class discusses how the shift changes the line's emotional weight before students attempt it themselves.

In small groups, students take the four lines from p.189–190 and rehearse delivering each with the indicated stress and intonation pattern. Groups experiment with alternative stresses and note how the emotional impact changes; one student per group presents a chosen delivery to the class.

Whole-class discussion: students identify which line was hardest to deliver convincingly and why. Teacher draws out the principle that stress and intonation carry character intention, not just information — connecting the exercise back to the asides and stage directions already encountered in the play.

periods.teacher_notes: The line 'Each bay, its own wind' works well as a final test of intonation because students must decide which word carries the primary stress to convey the play's thematic meaning rather than a merely descriptive sense. Encourage students who are hesitant to perform by having them deliver the line to a partner first before addressing the group.

periods.activity_title: Creating a Play Script: Anuradha's Dilemma

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.190–191): groups of four write a play script based on Anuradha's story — rough draft, setting, colon, brackets, aside, fillers, ellipsis

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Anuradha story opening aloud (p.190–191) and displays the six script-writing tips on the board: setting, colon after speaker, brackets for stage directions, aside, non-lexical fillers, and ellipsis for pauses. Groups of four decide on their characters and one key scene before writing begins.

Groups draft their play script, with the teacher circulating to ensure each group includes at least one aside and one stage direction in brackets. Teacher prompts groups to use a non-lexical filler at a moment of hesitation and an ellipsis at a moment of dramatic pause.

Each group nominates a reader who performs one short exchange from their script aloud. The class identifies — by show of hands — whether each script included an aside, a stage direction, and a filler. Groups revise any missing element in the final minutes so every script is complete before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The Anuradha scenario deliberately parallels Shruti's dilemma — a young musician, a disapproving father, a supportive family member — so students have strong thematic scaffolding without being asked to rewrite Twin Melodies itself. The most common gap in student scripts is the aside: remind groups that the aside must be marked '(Aside)' and delivered as if the other characters cannot hear it.

periods.activity_title: Play Script Conventions, Recycled Instruments and Indigenous Heritage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.192): study play-script conventions — no inverted commas, colons, brackets, actor guidance
Learning Beyond the Text (p.192): explore indigenous instruments from own region made from natural materials
Learning Beyond the Text (p.192–193): in groups, create a rhythm using objects around them and present

time_bands.activity: Students study the sample play-script dialogue on p.192 and answer the four convention questions — why no inverted commas, where colons appear, what brackets contain, and how stage directions help actors. Teacher consolidates the four answers as a brief reference guide students can use when they revisit their own scripts.

Teacher shares the Recycled Orchestra of Cateura information (p.192–193) as a brief context-setting moment, then opens the discussion: students name indigenous instruments from their own region, describe the materials they are made from, and connect this to the cultural-heritage theme of the play.

Groups of five select objects in the classroom — desks, water bottles, pencil cases — to create a short rhythm pattern and present it to the class. Each group names the 'instruments' they used and reflects briefly on what makes an object musical.

periods.teacher_notes: The rhythm-making activity links directly to the play's argument that musical creativity does not require formal instruments — an idea Nabin eventually concedes. If the classroom is very constrained on space or objects, the teacher may nominate two or three groups to present sequentially rather than simultaneously.
materials: Textbook pp.192–193 (Learning Beyond the Text, Twin Melodies)

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Tradition, Modernity and Each Bay Its Own Wind

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: 'Which single moment in the play most powerfully resolves the tension between tradition and modernity?' Students write a one-sentence answer with a reason, then share in pairs. Teacher takes three contrasting answers and notes them without adjudicating — this is the frame for the unit.

Structured debate — two sides argue whether Nabin's change of heart is convincing or whether it is too convenient a resolution. Each side draws on character-arc evidence from all three acts: Nabin's contempt in Act II, his tapping feet and clapping in Act III, and Leela's revelation about his own past defiance.

Students write a single well-organised paragraph — individually — that justifies the play's title 'Twin Melodies'. The paragraph must name at least two specific moments from the play and use one vocabulary or grammar point encountered during the chapter: a reported-speech construction, a music-domain term, or a figurative phrase.

Two or three students read their paragraphs aloud. The class identifies whether the twin 'melodies' each student named are the same or different — tradition and modernity, Shruti's violin and her father's past, or another pairing — and discusses which reading of the title feels richest. Teacher closes by naming the play's central insight: 'each bay, its own wind' as a universal statement about artistic identity.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the full arc of the play — from Shruti's aside in Act I to Nabin's admission and Leela's revelation in Act III — and can be run with any class that has covered the three acts, regardless of which earlier units they experienced. The debate and the paragraph are both self-contained: no draft from a previous unit is continued here.
materials: Rough-draft paper for the synthesis paragraph

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation and dramatic conflict by close-reading a play.
items.source_context: Shruti's fear of telling Nabin about the fusion concert and Nabin's Act II refusal.
items.item_stem: In Act II of Twin Melodies, Nabin tells Shruti that playing fusion music means 'drowning her individual style in the hubbub of an orchestra.' Which of the following best describes Nabin's primary concern?

options.label: A
options.text: He believes Shruti lacks the technical skill to perform alongside Western instruments.

options.label: B
options.text: He fears that fusion music will erode Shruti's distinct classical identity as a violinist.

options.label: C
options.text: He objects to the fusion group because he dislikes Iqbal, Avinash, and Peter personally.

options.label: D
options.text: He is worried that performing publicly will harm Shruti's academic studies.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be conflating Nabin's general scepticism about fusion with a specific skills doubt he never voices.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has misread Nabin's principled objection as a personal grievance against the group members.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has imported a common parental concern not present in the play's dialogue.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation and dramatic conflict by close-reading a play.
items.source_context: Shruti's fear of telling Nabin about the fusion concert and Nabin's Act II refusal.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

1. What does Nabin's admission 'I underestimated the power of our own music' reveal about the real source of his earlier resistance to fusion?
2. Leela reveals in Act III that Nabin himself defied his traditional vocalist family to take up the violin. How does this parallel history change the way you read Nabin's behaviour in Act II?
3. Evaluate the effectiveness of the play's ending: does the resolution feel earned, or is Nabin's transformation too swift? Justify your view with two specific moments from the play.
items.visual_stimulus:
Nabin (after listening to the fusion rehearsal, clapping): You never lost sight of the raga notes, Shruti. Not once. I underestimated the power of our own music. I was afraid you would be lost to us. I trust you, Shruti, and I will root for your group at the concert.
Leela (aside to Shruti): Your father defied his own family — a household of traditional vocalists — to take up the violin. He worked his fingers to the bone. He knows what it is to choose your own path.

expected_elements: Nabin feared classical music's identity would be diluted, not fusion itself.
The parallel shows Nabin's Act II rigidity mirrors his family's past resistance to him.
Students should name Act II refusal and Act III clapping as the two arc-moments.
A convincing evaluation judges whether the transformation is internally motivated.
Credit any well-reasoned position on whether the ending is satisfying.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening and note-taking from an oral description of a cultural artefact.
items.source_context: A musician's spoken description of the ancient yazh — its design, heritage and named varieties.
items.item_stem: Listen to the musician's description of the yazh. Then select all the statements that are true.

options.text: The yazh is described as the ancestor of the modern-day veena.
The yazh used metal strings stretched over a stone resonator.
The instrument was tuned using pegs or rings of gut moved along the strings.
One variety of the yazh was named after a peacock.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: the yazh used gut strings and a wooden, boat-shaped, skin-covered resonator — not metal strings or a stone resonator.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening and note-taking from an oral description of a cultural artefact.
items.source_context: A musician's spoken description of the ancient yazh — its design, heritage and named varieties.
items.item_stem: The musician explains that the yazh took different names depending on its design. In your own words, explain why an instrument might receive different names across its design variations, and reflect on what the example of the yazh suggests about the relationship between cultural heritage and musical innovation.

expected_elements: Recognises that design variations (peacock, crocodile, fish, bow) reflect different cultural symbols.
Connects naming to the communities and contexts in which the instrument was used.
Draws the inference that heritage is not fixed but evolves through creative adaptation.
Links this insight to the play's theme of tradition coexisting with new forms.

items.source_lo: Student uses stress and intonation purposefully to convey character emotion in dramatic speech.
items.source_context: Selected lines from Twin Melodies including Shruti's loyalty declaration and Nabin's aphorism.
items.item_stem: Read the following line aloud from Twin Melodies: 'Tonight, at dinner, I promise to bring this up.' Deliver the line twice — first with the stress on 'promise', then with the stress on 'tonight'. Explain to your teacher how the change in stress shifts the emotional meaning of the line.

expected_elements: Delivers both readings with a distinct, audible stress difference.
Explains that stressing 'promise' emphasises Shruti's determination.
Explains that stressing 'tonight' adds urgency — the deadline feels immediate.
Uses appropriate pace and a rising or falling intonation that fits each reading.

items.source_lo: Student uses stress and intonation purposefully to convey character emotion in dramatic speech.
items.source_context: Selected lines from Twin Melodies including Shruti's loyalty declaration and Nabin's aphorism.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will assign you either Nabin's role or Shruti's role. Argue your character's position in the Act II confrontation — Nabin arguing that classical tradition must not be compromised, or Shruti arguing that fusion honours rather than erases that tradition. Speak for at least one minute, using reasons drawn from the play, and respond to one challenge from your teacher.

expected_elements: Speaks in character, using the play's established motivation for that role.
Provides at least two reasons grounded in the play's events or dialogue.
Uses formal or elevated register appropriate to a reasoned argument.
Responds to the teacher's challenge with a direct counter-argument.
Maintains a coherent, audible delivery throughout.

items.source_lo: Student creates an original play script applying dramatic conventions and literary devices.
items.source_context: A young musician facing a disapproving parent decides to perform at a prestigious cultural event.
items.item_stem: Write a short notice (60–80 words) to be displayed on your school noticeboard, inviting students to a lunchtime listening session where recordings of classical Indian instruments — including the veena, sarod, and tabla — will be played. Include the date, venue, time, and purpose of the event.

expected_elements: Uses standard notice format: heading, date, venue, time.
States the purpose clearly — introducing students to classical Indian instruments.
Maintains a formal, inviting tone appropriate for a school notice.
Stays within the 60–80 word limit.

items.source_context: A young musician facing a disapproving parent decides to perform at a prestigious cultural event.
items.item_stem: Write a letter to your school magazine (150–180 words) arguing that school music programmes should include both classical Indian and contemporary forms of music. Your letter must present a reasoned argument, acknowledge a counter-view, and use at least one dramatic or musical image to support your case.

expected_elements: Uses letter-to-editor format: salutation, body paragraphs, sign-off.
States a clear, reasoned argument for including both musical forms.
Acknowledges and responds to the counter-view (e.g. diluting classical tradition).
Incorporates a dramatic or musical image — metaphor, allusion, or analogy.
Maintains formal register throughout and stays within the word limit.

items.item_stem:
The following lines are from Twin Melodies. Rewrite each one in reported speech, making all necessary changes to tense, pronoun, and reporting verb. Remove any interjection or exclamation mark.

1. Avinash (to Shruti): "Wow, you are a sensation now! The least you can do is throw a party!"
2. Nabin (at the dinner table): "I will not allow this kind of performance. Fusion music is not for serious musicians."
3. Leela (to Shruti, quietly): "Your father worked his fingers to the bone to succeed as a violinist."

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Avinash exclaimed with admiration that Shruti was a sensation and added that the least she could do was throw a party. 2. Nabin declared firmly that he would not allow that kind of performance and stated that fusion music was not for serious musicians. 3. Leela told Shruti quietly that her father had worked his fingers to the bone to succeed as a violinist.

items.item_stem: In a play script, dialogue is set out differently from dialogue in a prose story. Explain three conventions of play-script formatting — covering the use of colons, the absence of inverted commas, and the function of stage directions in brackets — and explain how each convention helps the reader or actor.

expected_elements: Correctly explains the colon as separating speaker's name from dialogue.
Explains absence of inverted commas: speaker is already identified, quotes are redundant.
Explains brackets as the space for stage directions — setting, action, tone.
Links each convention to a practical benefit for actor or reader.

items.item_stem: Design a project to document ONE indigenous musical instrument from your region or state. Your project plan must include: (a) how you will gather information (sources, people you will speak to, or visits you will make); (b) what aspects of the instrument you will document (materials, origin, cultural significance, playing technique); (c) how you will present your findings to the class (format and any materials you will make or use). Write your plan in 120–150 words.

expected_elements: Names a specific indigenous instrument from a real regional tradition.
Identifies at least two credible sources — person, library, community, or field visit.
Covers at least three aspects: materials, origin, cultural significance, or playing technique.
Proposes a clear presentation format — poster, oral report, demonstration, or script.
Writes in coherent, organised prose within the word limit.
